title: What is an access token vs refresh token: access token is short-lived for API access; refresh token is long-lived to get a new access token without re-login: and what is refresh token rotation?
shortTitle: Access Token vs Refresh Token and Refresh Token Rotation
keyPoints: An access token is short-lived (about 15 minutes), self-contained (JWT), and sent on every API call for authorization.
A refresh token is long-lived (days or weeks), stored server-side in hashed form, and used only to obtain a new access token.
The access token is validated statelessly by checking signature and expiry; the refresh token is validated by server-side lookup.
Refresh token rotation issues a new refresh token on every use and invalidates the old one, making it single-use.
Reuse detection: if an already-used refresh token is presented, the server revokes the entire token family, forcing re-login.
The refresh token must be stored in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie, never in localStorage.

s1_definition.oneliner: Short-lived access token for every call, long-lived refresh token to renew it, and rotate the refresh token so theft is single-use and detectable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Access token** – a short-lived credential (typically 15 minutes) presented on every API call to prove authorization; kept small and self-contained (JWT) so services validate it statelessly.
- **Refresh token** – a long-lived credential (days or weeks) used only to obtain a fresh access token from the auth server; stored server-side in hashed form and tightly guarded.
- **Refresh token rotation** – each time a refresh token is used, the server issues a new one and invalidates the old one, making it single-use.
- **Reuse detection** – if an already-used refresh token is ever presented again, that signals theft; the server revokes the entire token family and forces re-login.
s1_definition.analogy: The access token is like a visitor pass at National Bank of India that lets Rajesh move around for only fifteen minutes before it must be renewed. The refresh token is like the master membership card he keeps safely in his wallet; when his short pass expires he shows the membership card at the desk and gets a fresh fifteen-minute pass without signing in again. With rotation, every time he uses the membership card the desk shreds it and hands him a new one, so if a thief copied his old card, the moment either the thief or Rajesh uses it, the bank notices two cards claiming to be the same and locks the account.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Token Lifecycle:
  ┌────────┐  login    ┌─────────────┐
  │ Client ├──────────►│ Auth Server │
  │(Rajesh)│           │             │
  │        │◄──────────┤ Issues:     │
  │        │           │ Access (15m)│
  │        │           │ Refresh (7d)│
  └───┬────┘           └─────────────┘
      │
      │  Access token on every API call
      ▼
  ┌──────────────┐
  │Resource Server│ validates signature + expiry
  └──────────────┘

  When access token expires:
  ┌────────┐  refresh    ┌─────────────┐
  │ Client ├────────────►│ Auth Server │
  │        │  old RT     │             │
  │        │             │ Validates   │
  │        │◄────────────┤ Rotates:    │
  │        │  new AT +   │ Old RT used │
  │        │  new RT     │ New RT out  │
  └────────┘             └─────────────┘
```

```text
  Refresh Token Rotation + Reuse Detection:

  Normal:  RT-1 ──► rotate ──► RT-2 ──► rotate ──► RT-3
           (used)              (used)              (active)

  Theft:   RT-1 ──► rotate ──► RT-2 (sent to user)
            │
            └──► Thief replays RT-1 (already used!)
                 │
                 ▼
           REUSE DETECTED!
           Revoke entire family.
           RT-2 also killed.
           Force re-login.
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
An access token is a short-lived credential, typically about fifteen minutes, that the client sends on every API call to prove authorization, and it is kept small and self-contained so services can validate it statelessly. A refresh token is a long-lived credential, often days or weeks, whose only job is to obtain a new access token from the auth server without forcing the user to log in again. The split gives both safety and convenience: the constantly-used token has a tiny leak window, while the rarely-used token keeps the user signed in.

In the National Bank of India mobile app, the access token is sent on every request and, when it expires, the app quietly exchanges the refresh token for a new access token in the background, so Rajesh never sees a login screen during the day. The access token is a JWT validated by signature and expiry, while the refresh token is stored server-side in hashed form so it can be revoked, and in the browser it lives in an HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookie rather than localStorage.

Refresh token rotation is the part that matters most. Every time a refresh token is used, the server issues a brand-new refresh token and marks the old one used, so a given refresh token works at most once. If an already-used refresh token is ever presented again, that is a strong signal of theft, so the server revokes the entire token family and forces a fresh login.

The design turns a stolen refresh token from a long-lived master key into a single-use, quickly-detected incident, which is exactly the guarantee a bank needs.

Remember one sentence: short-lived access tokens limit the leak window, long-lived refresh tokens keep the session alive, and rotation ensures a stolen refresh token works at most once.
